notes:
I've written notes for all eight verses below. Most of the material comes from older commentaries, Enduring Word (Guzik), Calvin, Spurgeon and Augustine. The traditions really part ways at only one place, verse 7, over whether "them" means God's words or God's people.

**Superscription ("According to Sheminith")**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the meaning of the term is uncertain. It thinks the psalm was probably written while David lived at Saul's court, and it outlines the psalm as a complaint (vv. 1–2), a threat (vv. 3–4) and a promise (vv. 5–8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Guzik reads the title as naming the instrument, an eight-stringed harp. He says the psalm sets David's enemies' vicious words against God's pure word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- *Catholic/patristic:* Augustine reads "the eighth" as standing for the day of judgment or the eternal age that follows this present seven-day cycle. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801012.htm

**v. 1**
- Pulpit: "Help" is better translated "Save." "Ceaseth" means gone from the land, killed or driven into exile. Allow for poetic exaggeration: for the moment the writer loses sight of the remnant that he mentions again in vv. 5 and 7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Ellicott: the Hebrew word for "faithful" is related to "amen." Luther rendered it as people who are as good as their word. https://biblehub.com/psalms/12-1.htm
- Barnes and Benson: the word "godly" (*chasid*) properly means the kind or merciful man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/12-1.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist): "Help, Lord" is a short prayer to use in any emergency. When godly people die, leave or fall away, that should be a call to pray more. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps012.cfm
- Guzik: we don't know when David wrote it. He felt alone against gossip and backbiting and took his case to the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- Reformed (via TGC): Calvin says the lament is not about outsiders but about a "deluge of iniquity" inside God's church. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/help-hope-leaders-fall/

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: "vanity" here means falsehood. "Double heart" is literally "a heart and a heart." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Guzik: flattering lips tell people what they want to hear, and this happens in churches too. He quotes a writer who says a man with two hearts is a monster. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- Augustine likewise takes "a heart and a heart" as a double heart. He reads "neighbour" as meaning every person. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801012.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: after the complaint comes a threat. Flatterers will be "cut off" from the congregation. One and the same man may sweet-talk at one moment and boast at the next. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Guzik: David felt helpless against these talkers, so he appealed to God. He quotes Maclaren: better to have the tongue touched with a live coal than cut out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- Augustine: "all" is there so that nobody thinks he is the exception. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801012.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: these men think they can get anything by persuasion, threats or clever argument. "Our lips are with us" means our lips are on our side. They don't believe any righteous Judge will step in. Its homily on this verse adds that our lips are not our own because we are not our own (1 Cor 6:19–20). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Guzik: for a Christian, the answer to "who is lord over us?" is Jesus, who owns us body, soul and spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- Augustine: the verse describes proud hypocrites who trust their speech to deceive people and will not submit to God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801012.htm

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: having threatened the wicked, God now promises to help the oppressed. He will "now," at last, arise, as in Exod 3:7–8. It prefers the translation "the safety for which he pants." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Guzik: the proud talkers could not stop God from speaking. David took the promise as meant for him, one of the needy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- The Biblical Illustrator presents God's word in v. 5 as the answer to the prayer of v. 1. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-12.html

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: God's words contain no worthless metal mixed in, so what God promises he will do. "Furnace of earth" may mean a crucible on the ground. Its homily says God has already separated out the dross, and that the Bible has survived both believers' experience and hostile criticism. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Ellicott calls a scholar's proposed correction of "earth" to "bar" (silver melted into a bar) "almost convincing." https://biblehub.com/psalms/12-6.htm
- Barnes contrasts men who cannot be relied on with God's statements, which can be trusted completely. JFB says "seven times" means thoroughly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/12-6.htm
- Augustine: "pure" means without pretence. He contrasts it with those who preach truth impurely, for gain (Phil 1). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801012.htm

**v. 7: the one real disagreement (them / us / him)**
- **Words of God:** Guzik reads v. 7 as God preserving his own words through the centuries. He cites VanGemeren for manuscript support for "them," quotes Morgan that "them" means the words, and concludes that God keeps both his Word and his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- **People of God, Reformed:** Calvin rejects the "words" reading and says David returns to the poor. The switch from "them" to "him" is normal Hebrew, though it may hint at how few the godly are. He also allows the verse could be read as a prayer. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol08/htm/xviii.iv.htm
- **People of God, Baptist:** Gill also rejects "words" because the pronoun is masculine, not feminine. He grants that God has kept Scripture, but reads the verse as God keeping the needy "from a total and final falling away." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/12-7.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch say the Hebrew is "him," not "us." Pulpit says "him" sums up the whole class of the righteous. Poole and Benson take both sides: God keeps his promises and his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/12-7.htm
- Matthew Henry: God will keep his remnant from being corrupted or wiped out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/12-7.html
- **Ancient versions:** Clarke notes that several manuscripts, the Septuagint and the Vulgate read "us." Calvin's notes add that the Aramaic paraphrase reads "the just." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/12-7.html. The Catholic Douay-Rheims translation has "preserve us." https://biblehub.com/kjv/psalms/12-7.htm
- **Modern debate:** a Bible Hub Q&A asks how this verse fits with copying variations in manuscripts. It answers that either way the stress is on God's faithful character. https://biblehub.com/q/why_promise_preservation_if_text_changed.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: read it as "while" or "though" the wicked roam freely and villainy exalts itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-12.html
- Guzik: God's word doesn't remove the wicked, but they never have the assurance of final victory. The ending is realistic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-12/
- Spurgeon: an exalted sinner encourages other sinners, so our exalted Redeemer should spur his saints on. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps012.cfm

**What I couldn't find:**
- NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, catholic.com and OCA pages on this psalm.
- Pages from the Methodist, Pentecostal or Lutheran sites specifically on Psalm 12.
- Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it.
- A page on these sites that sets out the King James Only use of v. 7.
